title: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
summary: From activation patching and QK/OV circuits to attribution graphs: build a linear graph of features for one prompt, prune it by influence, validate it with interventions, and know where it breaks.
outcomes: Run activation patching with a logit-difference metric and explain when noising and denoising disagree
Split an attention head into QK and OV circuits and explain how an induction head composes two heads
Explain why connecting SAE features across an MLP has no fixed edge weight, and how transcoders fix it
Build a local replacement model: CLT features, frozen attention and norms, and error nodes
Compute attribution edges, logit influence, edge scores and completeness for a small graph
Validate a graph with interventions and explain why large perturbations do not add
Identify what graphs miss, including QK circuits, error nodes and inactive features, and how QK attribution helps
Trace, label and intervene on a real graph with circuit-tracer, and report what was and was not validated

lessons.title: Why tracing circuits needs a replacement model

blocks.md:
Recall from the sparse autoencoder course: an SAE rewrites a dense activation vector as a sparse sum of **features**, directions that often match human concepts. Features tell you *what* a model represents at one point. A **circuit** says *how* those features combine, step by step, to produce a particular output.

This course teaches **attribution graphs** (Anthropic, 2025): a graph, built for one prompt, whose nodes are features and whose edges say how much each feature pushed each later feature and the output logit. A logit is the raw score the model gives one candidate next token before the softmax turns all the scores into probabilities. Anthropic published the method in March 2025 as two companion papers: a methods paper, Circuit Tracing, which builds the graphs, and a biology paper, On the Biology of a Large Language Model, which uses them to study Claude 3.5 Haiku. This course cites them as the methods paper and the biology paper.

The older workhorse for finding circuits is **activation patching**. Run the model on a *clean* prompt and on a *corrupted* prompt that changes the answer. Copy one component's activation (an attention head, an MLP layer) from one run into the other, and measure how a metric such as the logit difference between the two answers moves.

Wang et al. (2022) used a refinement called *path patching* on GPT-2 small for indirect object identification: given "When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to", predict "Mary". The indirect object is the person receiving the drink. Path patching patches a component's output only along one chosen route, for example only where it feeds a particular later head, so it shows which connections between components matter, not just which components. Their explanation involved 26 attention heads in 7 classes, such as Name Mover heads and S-Inhibition heads. Name Mover heads attend to the names and copy the right one, Mary, into the output. S-Inhibition heads, where S stands for the subject John, who appears twice, signal the Name Movers to stop attending to John.

blocks.title: Activation patching on one component

nodes.label:
clean prompt
...John gave a drink to

scenes.caption: Two forward passes: a clean prompt where the answer is Mary, and a corrupted prompt where it changes. The metric is the logit of one answer minus the other.
Patch one component: copy its activation from the clean run into the corrupted run and rerun. If the metric recovers, that component carries the needed information.
One patch costs one forward pass, and the answer is about a whole head or MLP. A head that does many unrelated jobs across the data gives a coarse explanation.

blocks.md:
Patching is causal and reliable, but it has three costs that matter for tracing:

- **Coarse units.** Heads and MLP blocks play many unrelated roles across the data, and individual neurons are polysemantic, so a patched component is not a clean concept.
- **Cost.** Each component needs its own forward pass. Attribution patching swaps this for a linear (gradient) approximation: one backward pass gives the gradient of the metric with respect to every activation, and the estimated effect of patching a component is that gradient dotted with the difference between its clean and corrupted activations, a first-order Taylor estimate. Syed et al. (2023) use it to score every edge with two forward passes and one backward pass.
- **A designed counterfactual.** You need a corrupted prompt, and the answer depends on which one you pick.

The next lesson works through the cost and the choice of counterfactual with real numbers from GPT-2 small; the coarse units are what transcoders and attribution graphs fix after that.

Why not connect SAE features directly? Put an SAE before an MLP and another after it. A feature before the MLP influences a feature after it only *through* the MLP, where it is mixed into many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity. Dunefsky et al. describe exactly this obstacle: features are linear combinations of extremely many neurons, so circuit analysis through MLPs becomes intractable. The size of the effect depends on what else is active, so there is no single edge weight to write down. [Sparse feature circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19647) (Marks et al., 2024) did connect SAE features this way, but each edge is a gradient estimate around one input, with the MLP still inside it.

blocks.prompt: Toy setup: a source SAE feature feeds a 4-neuron GELU MLP, and a target SAE feature reads the MLP output. Scaling the source by 1 moves the target by 0.362. If you scale the source by 3, does the target move by about 3 x 0.362 = 1.09?
blocks.reveal: No. In this toy MLP (weights chosen by hand, computed with a script) the target moves by **2.846**, about 2.6 times the linear guess. Some neurons were below their bend at scale 1 and switch on at larger scales. Through an MLP, "how much does A drive B" has no single answer.

blocks.title: Effect on a target feature through a GELU MLP (toy)

scenes.caption: The linear guess: if the effect at x1 is 0.362, a straight line predicts 0.181, 0.362, 0.724 and 1.085.
The actual effect through the MLP: 0.071, 0.362, 1.505, 2.846. Same toy weights, computed exactly. The MLP's nonlinearity makes the edge depend on the input, so no fixed edge weight exists.

blocks.md:
The fix has two parts, and the rest of the course unpacks them:

1. Replace each MLP with a **transcoder**, whose sparse features *are* the computation, so features can feed features directly.
2. For one fixed prompt, **freeze** the remaining nonlinearities (attention patterns and normalization denominators) at their observed values. An attention pattern is the set of softmax weights a head puts on earlier positions, and it depends on the input. Normalization layers such as LayerNorm divide each residual vector by its own size (its standard deviation or root mean square), so that denominator also depends on the input. Once both are fixed numbers for this prompt, they become constants.

Then every direct effect between features is linear and has a well-defined size. The full pipeline: train a cross-layer transcoder, build a local replacement model for the prompt, compute edges, prune, label and group features, and validate with interventions in the real model.

Attribution graphs trade the real model for an interpretable stand-in whose direct interactions are linear on one prompt. Every claim read off the graph is a hypothesis about the real model until an intervention confirms it.

blocks.question: A team runs activation patching on every attention head of a 24-layer model with 16 heads per layer. Which statement about this experiment is correct?
options: It needs one forward pass per patched head, and each result describes a whole head rather than a concept
It needs a single backward pass in total and returns feature-level edges
It needs no corrupted prompt because patching compares a run with itself
It gives the same answer for any choice of corrupted prompt
blocks.explain: Each patch is its own forward pass (384 heads here), and the unit of explanation is the whole head, which may do many jobs. The answer also depends on the corrupted prompt you chose. Attribution patching cuts the cost with a linear approximation; attribution graphs change the units to sparse features.

blocks.question: Why can't you assign one fixed weight to the edge from an SAE feature before an MLP to an SAE feature after it?
options: SAE features are always dense, so the weight would be huge
The two SAEs use different dictionary sizes
The effect passes through many MLP neurons with nonlinearities, so its size depends on everything else active
Attention moves the feature to a different token position
blocks.explain: The MLP mixes the source direction into many neurons, each with a nonlinearity, so the downstream effect changes with the input, as the toy showed (2.846 instead of 1.085 at scale 3). Transcoders sidestep this by replacing the MLP itself with sparse features.

lessons.title: Activation patching worked through: two directions and a shortcut

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 sketched activation patching. Here it is with real numbers, so that the contrast with attribution graphs later is concrete.

Take the prompt "When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to". GPT-2 small, the 124M-parameter model from the build-a-GPT course, puts probability 0.677 on " Mary" and 0.023 on " John". Change the second name and the **corrupted** prompt "... Mary gave a drink to" flips the preference: 0.034 on Mary and 0.411 on John. Everything else, length included (15 tokens), stays the same.

The code uses TransformerLens, a library started by Neel Nanda that exposes every intermediate activation of GPT-2 as a named hook point you can read or overwrite during a forward pass. `hook_z` holds each head's attention-weighted value vectors, just before the output matrix $W_O$ mixes the heads back into the residual stream.

The **logit difference** $LD = \text{logit}(\text{Mary}) - \text{logit}(\text{John})$ is 3.362 on the clean prompt and -2.479 on the corrupted one. Heimersheim and Nanda recommend it as the default patching metric for two reasons. The residual stream is a sum of component outputs and the logits are, up to the final normalization, a linear function of it, so each component's contribution simply adds. And comparing two names ignores components that raise every name at once, such as a "the next token is a name" circuit.

To compare patches across components, rescale it so the corrupted run scores 0 and the clean run scores 1:

blocks.caption: 0 means no better than the corrupted run, 1 means fully clean behavior. A component that fights the answer can push the score below 0.

blocks.md:
The corrupted prompt decides what you can find: patching only reveals components that care about what changed between the two prompts. Swapping which name repeats, as here, traces where the model tracks who the indirect object is. Replacing names with unrelated ones would trace where name values are stored instead. Wang et al. ran their path patching against the **ABC distribution**, the same sentence templates filled with three unrelated random names, so no plausible indirect object remains while the grammar stays intact.

There are also two directions to patch in:

- **Denoising** (clean into corrupted): run the corrupted prompt and overwrite one activation with its clean value. A rising score says the component is *sufficient* to restore the behavior.
- **Noising** (corrupted into clean): run the clean prompt and overwrite one activation with its corrupted value. A falling score says the component is *necessary*.

blocks.code:
import torch
from transformer_lens import HookedTransformer   # TransformerLens 3.x API
model = HookedTransformer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
clean   = model.to_tokens("When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to")
corrupt = model.to_tokens("When Mary and John went to the store, Mary gave a drink to")
mary, john = model.to_single_token(" Mary"), model.to_single_token(" John")
ld = lambda lg: (lg[0, -1, mary] - lg[0, -1, john]).item()
clean_logits, clean_cache = model.run_with_cache(clean)
LD_clean, LD_corr = ld(clean_logits), ld(model(corrupt))      # 3.362, -2.479
score = torch.zeros(12, 12)
for l in range(12):
    for h in range(12):
        def patch(z, hook, h=h):              # z: [batch, pos, head, d_head]
            z[:, :, h] = clean_cache[hook.name][:, :, h]
            return z
        lg = model.run_with_hooks(corrupt, fwd_hooks=[(f"blocks.{l}.attn.hook_z", patch)])
        score[l, h] = (ld(lg) - LD_corr) / (LD_clean - LD_corr)
print(score[8, 10], score[9, 9], score[10, 7])   # tensor(0.2527) tensor(0.2448) tensor(-0.4606)
blocks.caption: Denoising every head of GPT-2 small, one forward pass per head (144 in total). Run here on a CPU; the printed values are the real output. Needs TransformerLens 3 (pip install "transformer-lens<4"): version 4 removed HookedTransformer in favor of TransformerBridge.

blocks.title: Patching each head of GPT-2 small on one IOI prompt pair

scenes.caption: Denoising score per head (row = layer, column = head). The largest are 8.10 (0.25), 9.9 (0.25), 8.6 (0.22), 7.9 and 5.5 (0.18) and 7.3 (0.14). No single head restores more than a quarter of the behavior.

These match Wang et al.'s classes: 7.3, 7.9, 8.6 and 8.10 are S-Inhibition heads, 9.9 a Name Mover, 5.5 an induction head (lesson 4). Heads 10.7 (-0.46) and 11.10 (-0.18) are their Negative Name Movers, which push against the answer.

Noising: the drop (1 minus score) when one head gets its corrupted value inside the clean run. On this prompt pair the two directions agree closely (correlation 0.96 across heads), with the same top heads.

blocks.md:
Why can the two directions disagree? Heimersheim and Nanda's example: components A and B feed C, and only C reaches the output.

- If C = A AND B, denoising A alone does nothing, because B is still corrupted. Only denoising C restores the output. Noising A, B or C each breaks it, so noising finds all three.
- If C = A OR B, it flips: denoising A, B or C each restores the output, while noising A alone does nothing because B still carries the clean signal.

Real models contain both shapes: serial dependence (a later head needs an earlier one) acts like AND, and redundant backup heads act like OR.

blocks.title: AND and OR gates under the two patching directions (toy)

scenes.caption: C = AND(A, B), written as max(A + B - 1, 0), with clean A = B = 1 and corrupted A = B = 0. Denoising one input recovers 0 of the behavior; only C recovers 1.
Same AND gate, noising: corrupting any one of A, B or C drops the output by the full amount. Noising found the whole circuit, denoising only its last step.
C = OR(A, B), written as min(A + B, 1). Denoising any one component restores the output fully.
OR gate, noising: corrupting A leaves B clean, so nothing breaks. A backup component hides from noising. Computed with the two formulas above.

blocks.prompt: In IOI, Wang et al. knocked out all three main Name Mover heads at once. Name Movers copy the answer name into the output. What do you expect happened to the logit difference?
blocks.reveal: It fell by only **5%**. Other heads, which Wang et al. named Backup Name Movers, took over the copying once the main ones were gone. That is the OR shape: each Name Mover looks less necessary than it is. Heimersheim and Nanda note backup is lossy (the Hydra effect paper measured about 0.7 of the original effect), so the original heads usually still show up, just weaker.

blocks.md: **Path patching** narrows a patch to one route. Normally a patched head changes everything downstream of it. In path patching the patched value reaches only one chosen receiver, for example only the queries of the Name Mover heads, and every other path keeps its old value. That separates "A affects the output through B" from "A affects the output directly". Wang et al. found the S-Inhibition heads this way: patching the path from 7.3, 7.9, 8.6 and 8.10 into the Name Movers' queries lowered the logit difference.

**Attribution patching** replaces the many forward passes with one gradient. Treat the corrupted run as locally linear in an activation $a$. Then the effect of patching $a$ from its corrupted value to its clean value is roughly the gradient of the metric at the corrupted run, dotted with the change:

blocks.caption: A first-order Taylor estimate. Two forward passes (to cache clean and corrupted activations) and one backward pass give it for every activation at once.

blocks.title: When the linear estimate of a patch breaks (toy)

scenes.caption: A unit with a saturating output, corrupted value 0.2. Patching to a clean value of 0.5 truly adds 0.794; the tangent line predicts 0.865. Close: small patches are where attribution patching works.

Patch to a clean value of 2.5 and the unit saturates: the true change is 2.368, but the tangent predicts 6.631, nearly 3 times too big. Large patches through a flattening nonlinearity are where the estimate breaks.

blocks.md:
On the real heads above, the gradient estimate is good: computed from the same two forward passes plus one backward pass, it correlates 0.985 with the 144 true denoising scores (for example 0.257 vs 0.253 for head 8.10 and -0.402 vs -0.461 for 10.7). That matches Nanda's finding that the approximation works for small activations such as single head outputs and fails for large ones such as a whole residual stream or the first MLP layer.

Two tools push this toward automatic circuit discovery. **ACDC** (Conmy et al., 2023) prunes edges of the model's computational graph one by one, keeping an edge only if patching it changes the output enough; on GPT-2 small's greater-than task (completing "from the year 1732 to the year 17" with a later year) it kept 68 of 32,000 edges, all found earlier by hand. **Edge attribution patching** (Syed et al., 2023) scores every edge with the gradient estimate instead, in two forward and one backward pass. Attribution graphs keep that gradient idea, but swap heads for features and drop the corrupted prompt.

Denoising asks whether a component is enough to restore the behavior; noising asks whether the behavior needs it. AND-like circuits hide from denoising, OR-like backups hide from noising, and gradient shortcuts are trustworthy only for small patches.

blocks.question: Two heads feed a later head in series: the later head only works if both earlier heads carry the clean signal. You denoise each earlier head separately. What do you most likely see?
options: Each earlier head restores half of the behavior
Both earlier heads show strong recovery, the later head shows none
Denoising cannot be run on heads in series
Neither earlier head restores much, so denoising alone would miss them
blocks.explain: Serial dependence behaves like an AND gate. Patching one input leaves the other corrupted, so the downstream head stays off. Noising each earlier head would reveal them, since breaking either one breaks the output.

blocks.question: Attribution patching estimates a head's patch effect at 0.30, but the true activation patch gives 0.05. Which explanation fits best?
options: The corrupted prompt was too similar to the clean one
The patch moved the activation far along a nonlinearity, so the first-order estimate overshoots
Gradients cannot be taken with respect to activations
Logit difference is not linear in the logits
blocks.explain: The estimate is a tangent line at the corrupted run. If the patch is large or crosses a saturating or switching nonlinearity (softmax, LayerNorm, an MLP neuron), the true effect can be far from the tangent, as in the toy where it predicted 6.631 for a true 2.368.

blocks.md:
An SAE reads an activation and reconstructs *the same* activation. A **transcoder** reads the MLP's *input* and predicts the MLP's *output*. It is a wider, sparsely active MLP trained to imitate the dense one (Dunefsky et al., 2024).

That small change matters. An SAE describes what is present; a transcoder can *replace* the MLP, so its features are the computation itself. A feature's output then flows straight into later features' inputs, with no opaque MLP in between.

blocks.caption: x is the MLP input, y-hat the predicted MLP output. JumpReLU outputs h when h is above a learned threshold and 0 otherwise.

blocks.title: A 4-feature transcoder on one token (toy)
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.2, -0.4, 0.9])             # MLP input (residual stream)
W_enc = np.array([[ 0.8,  0.0,  0.6],      # 4 features x 3 dims
                  [ 0.0, -1.0,  0.2],
                  [ 0.5,  0.5, -0.5],
                  [-0.3,  0.4,  0.9]])
theta = 0.5                                 # JumpReLU threshold
W_dec = np.array([[ 0.6, 0.0, 0.2, -0.1],   # 3 dims x 4 features
                  [ 0.2, 0.5, 0.0,  0.4],
                  [-0.1, 0.3, 0.0,  0.7]])
y_mlp = np.array([0.95, 0.55, 0.08])        # true MLP output on this token

h = W_enc @ x                               # pre-activations
a = np.where(h > theta, h, 0.0)             # JumpReLU: keep h only above theta
y_hat = W_dec @ a                           # transcoder's guess at MLP output
err = y_mlp - y_hat                         # becomes the error node
print(h.round(3), a.round(3))
print(y_hat.round(3), err.round(3))

scenes.caption: Encode: each feature takes a dot product with the MLP input. Feature 0 gets 1.5, feature 1 gets 0.58, and the other two are low.
JumpReLU zeroes everything at or below the threshold 0.5. Only 2 of 4 features are active: that sparsity is what makes the graph small later. Simplified: real CLTs learn one threshold per feature.
Decode: the active features' decoder columns, weighted by activation, add up to the predicted MLP output.
The leftover between the true MLP output and the guess is the reconstruction error. Attribution graphs keep it as an error node so nothing is silently dropped.

blocks.md: A **cross-layer transcoder (CLT)** goes one step further. It has one set of features per model layer. A feature at layer $\ell$ reads the residual stream at layer $\ell$, but it writes to the MLP outputs of layer $\ell$ *and every later layer*, with a separate decoder for each. All layers are trained jointly, so the MLP output at layer $\ell'$ is reconstructed by features from all earlier layers together.

blocks.caption: The prediction for layer l's MLP output sums contributions from features living in layers 1 through l.

Reconstruction error summed over layers plus a sparsity penalty: lambda times the sum, over layers and features, of tanh of c times feature i's decoder norm times its activation. The decoder norm uses all of feature i's decoders concatenated; lambda and c are hyperparameters.

blocks.md: Why multiply the activation by the decoder norm? A feature's contribution to the output is its activation times its decoder vector. Without the norm, training could halve every activation and double every decoder: the output stays the same and the penalty drops for free. Weighting by the decoder norm penalizes the size of the actual contribution, so that trick no longer helps.

blocks.title: The tanh sparsity penalty saturates, unlike L1

scenes.caption: An L1-style penalty grows forever with activation, which shrinks large activations. The tanh penalty charges roughly the same for any clearly active feature, so it mostly counts how many features fire.
Raise c and the tanh curve becomes a near step: almost a count of active features (an L0 penalty) that still has gradients.

blocks.title: Per-layer chain vs one cross-layer feature

nodes.label:
Copenhagen L1
writes to L1, L2, L3

scenes.caption: With per-layer transcoders, a concept that the model amplifies over several layers shows up as a chain of near-identical features, each re-activating the next.

A CLT can learn one early feature that writes to all those layers at once, collapsing the chain. The methods paper reports a 7-step Copenhagen chain with per-layer transcoders that the CLT collapses to layer 1 features.
Shorter paths are easier to read: average path length 2.3 for a 10M-feature CLT vs 3.7 for 10M per-layer transcoders on one example prompt. Simplified: three layers drawn instead of eighteen.

blocks.md: Scale, from the methods paper: CLTs were trained on an 18-layer model ("18L", which has no MLP in layer 0, so its CLT has 17 layers) with 300K to 10M total features, and on Claude 3.5 Haiku with 300K to 30M. Swapping CLT outputs in for every MLP while running attention normally gives the **replacement model**. The largest 18L CLT made the same top next-token prediction as the real model on 50% of a diverse set of prompts (filtered to tokens the real model predicts correctly with under 80% confidence).

CLTs cost more per feature: the same encoder size as per-layer transcoders but about $n_{layers}/2$ times the decoder parameters. The count comes from the decoders: with L layers, a feature at layer 1 has L decoders, one at layer 2 has L minus 1, and so on down to 1. That sums to L times (L plus 1) over 2 decoders across the L layers, or (L plus 1) over 2 per feature on average, against 1 per feature for a per-layer transcoder. As a rough guide, the paper estimates a 2M-feature CLT on Gemma 2 2B with 1B training tokens at 3.8e20 FLOPs, or roughly 210 H100 hours: 210 hours of one Nvidia H100 graphics processing unit running at half its peak speed.

Collapsing chains is not free. If the real model really runs a mutually reinforcing loop (the paper sees Copenhagen and Denmark features exciting each other with per-layer transcoders), a CLT can hide it. Simpler graphs can mean less faithful graphs.

blocks.question: What does a transcoder learn to approximate?
options: The residual stream at the same layer, from itself
The output of an MLP layer, computed from that MLP's input
The attention pattern of every head in the layer
The final logits, computed from the embeddings
blocks.explain: A transcoder maps MLP input to MLP output through a wide sparse layer, so it can stand in for the MLP. An SAE reconstructs the same activation it reads, which describes but does not replace the computation.

blocks.question: Your graphs from per-layer transcoders show long chains of near-duplicate features across layers. What does switching to a CLT most likely change?
options: Nothing, because chains come from attention
The chains get longer because each layer now has more decoders
The chains collapse into fewer early features, at the risk of hiding a real multi-step loop
Error nodes disappear entirely
blocks.explain: A CLT feature writes to all later layers, so repeated amplification can be absorbed into one feature: shorter paths, but its causal structure can differ from the underlying model's. Error nodes remain because no dictionary is perfect.

lessons.title: Reading a transformer as circuits: residual paths, QK and OV

blocks.md:
Lesson 5 will say that an edge in an attribution graph is "a sum over paths through residual connections and frozen attention", and lesson 9 will say graphs miss "QK circuits" and "induction". This lesson builds that vocabulary from Elhage et al.'s *A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits* (2021).

Recall from the build-a-GPT course: each position keeps a vector, the **residual stream**, and every attention layer and MLP reads it and adds its output back. Elhage et al. call it a communication channel: it does no processing itself. A layer *reads* by a linear projection (multiplying by $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ or the MLP input matrix) and *writes* by addition. So the final vector is literally the embedding plus every layer's output.

Because writing is addition, the logits can be expanded into a sum over **paths**. Take the simplest case Elhage et al. analyze: one layer, attention only, no MLP. The logits are the unembedding of the embedding plus every head's output. Multiplying out gives one term per path: the **direct path** (embedding straight to unembedding, which can only learn which token follows which) plus one term per head. In the formula, $A^h$ is head h's attention pattern, a mix across positions, and $\otimes$ pairs it with a matrix that acts on each position's vector separately.

blocks.tex: T = \mathrm{Id} \otimes W_U W_E \;+\; \sum_{h} A^{h} \otimes \big(W_U W_{OV}^{h} W_E\big)
blocks.caption: One-layer attention-only transformer. W_E embeds tokens, W_U unembeds to logits. With two layers, extra terms appear for paths through two heads in a row (virtual heads).

blocks.title: The logits as a sum of paths

scenes.caption: The direct path: embedding to unembedding with nothing in between. On its own it can only learn bigram statistics.
One term per head: the embedding is read by a head, moved between positions by its attention pattern, and written to the logits. With one layer the logits are exactly these terms added up.
Add a second layer and a head can read what an earlier head wrote. Paths through two heads appear, and the number of paths grows with depth. This is the sum that a frozen-attention Jacobian adds up.

blocks.md:
Each head splits into two independent circuits. Its attention score from a query position with residual vector $x_q$ to a key position $x_k$ is $x_q^\top W_Q^\top W_K x_k$, so only the product $W_{QK} = W_Q^\top W_K$ matters: the **QK circuit**, which decides *where to attend*. What it writes when it attends to position k is $W_O W_V x_k$, so only $W_{OV} = W_O W_V$ matters: the **OV circuit**, which decides *what is copied*. Here $W_O$ is the head's output matrix that writes into the residual stream.

Elhage et al. point out the consequence used throughout this course: if you record the attention patterns once and then freeze them, the head's output is a linear function of its inputs, carried entirely by OV. QK has been turned into constants.

blocks.title: One head on two positions, as QK and OV (toy, d = 3)
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1., 0, 1],     # pos 0 "Sally": dims = name, Aunt, Sally-identity
              [0., 1, 0]])    # pos 1 "Aunt"
W_Q = np.array([[0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0.5]]);  W_K = np.array([[2., 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]])
W_V = np.array([[0, 0, 1.], [1, 0, 0]]);   W_O = np.array([[0, 0.5], [0, 0], [1.5, 0]])

W_QK = W_Q.T @ W_K            # 3 x 3: where to attend
W_OV = W_O @ W_V              # 3 x 3: what gets written
s = np.array([x[1] @ W_QK @ x[j] for j in (0, 1)]) / np.sqrt(2)
A = np.exp(s) / np.exp(s).sum()          # query = pos 1, keys = pos 0, 1
out = sum(A[j] * W_OV @ x[j] for j in (0, 1))
print(W_QK); print(W_OV)
print(s.round(3), A.round(3), out.round(3))

scenes.caption: Three-dimensional residual vectors. Position 0 holds "Sally" (a name, with an identity direction); position 1 holds "Aunt". The head has a two-dimensional query, key and value space.

Collapse the four weight matrices into two 3 x 3 ones. W_QK has a 2 in row Aunt, column name: an Aunt query looks for names. W_OV copies the Sally-identity direction (1.5) and the name direction (0.5).
Scores from the query at Aunt: 2 / sqrt(2) = 1.414 to Sally and 0 to itself. These equal the usual q dot k computed with the separate matrices.
Softmax gives 0.804 on Sally. The output is 0.804 times W_OV times the Sally vector: the head writes Sally's identity into the Aunt position.

blocks.md:
Heads in different layers can **compose**: a later head's query, key or value reads a subspace an earlier head wrote. Elhage et al. name these Q-, K- and V-composition. Q and K composition change *where* the later head attends; V composition chains two copies into a "virtual head".

The famous product of K-composition is the **induction head**. It completes patterns of the form [A][B] ... [A] by predicting [B]. Two heads cooperate:

1. A **previous-token head** copies each token's identity into the next position, so the position of B now also carries "preceded by A".
2. The induction head's query is the current token A; its key, built by K-composition from the previous-token head's output, matches "preceded by A". It attends to B, and its copying OV circuit writes B into the output.

blocks.title: Two real GPT-2 small heads on "I visited Aunt Sally. Later, Aunt"

scenes.caption: Head 4.11: each query row puts about 1.00 on the token just before it. On random repeated token sequences its average attention to the previous token is 0.99, the highest of all 144 heads. Wang et al. also list 4.11 as a previous-token head.

Head 5.5: most rows rest on the first token (a common no-op), but the last Aunt puts 0.90 on Sally, the token after the earlier Aunt. Its induction score on random repeats, 0.93, is the model's highest. GPT-2 then predicts Sally at 0.932.

blocks.md: Now connect this to attribution graphs. Freezing attention keeps the induction head's OV circuit, so the graph does show an edge from Sally features at the Sally position to say-Sally at the last position. It discards the QK circuit, so the reason the head looked at Sally (a previous-token head plus a key that matched Aunt) never appears. Lesson 5 makes the freezing precise, and lesson 9 returns to a longer version of this prompt.

A head is two circuits. QK, built from $W_Q^\top W_K$, picks where to look; OV, built from $W_O W_V$, picks what to copy. With patterns frozen, the whole model is a sum of linear paths through OV and residual connections.

blocks.prompt: You freeze all attention patterns in the GPT-2 run above, then change only the first "Sally" to "Susan" by editing its embedding. With attention frozen, roughly how will the induction head's output at the last position change?
blocks.reveal: Head 5.5 still puts 0.90 on position 4, which now holds Susan, and its OV circuit copies whatever is there. So the output moves toward Susan, linearly in the change to the vector the head reads at position 4 (the MLPs below it at that position are still nonlinear in the embedding). Frozen attention means the edge from that position is linear. Whether the *unfrozen* model would still attend there depends on QK: it should, since "preceded by Aunt" is unchanged, but that reasoning is exactly what a frozen-attention graph cannot show.

blocks.question: In Elhage et al.'s terms, which matrix decides which earlier position a head reads from?
options: $W_Q^\top W_K$, the QK circuit
$W_O W_V$, the OV circuit
$W_U W_E$, the direct path
The MLP's input matrix
blocks.explain: Attention scores are $x_q^\top W_Q^\top W_K x_k$, so the QK product alone sets where the head attends. OV decides what is written once it attends; the direct path never moves information between positions.

blocks.question: An induction head relies on K-composition with a previous-token head. What does the previous-token head contribute?
options: It writes the next token's identity into the current position
It sets the induction head's query to the previous token
It writes "preceded by A" into the position after A, which the induction head's key reads
It copies the answer token into the logits
blocks.explain: The previous-token head moves A's identity one position forward, so B's position carries "preceded by A". The induction head's key reads that, its query is the current A, and the match makes it attend to B and copy it.

lessons.title: The local replacement model makes every edge linear

blocks.md:
The replacement model alone still disagrees with the real model about half the time, and errors compound across layers. So for one fixed prompt $p$ the method builds a **local replacement model**:

1. Substitute the CLT for the MLPs.
2. Freeze the **attention patterns** and the **normalization denominators** at the values from the real model's forward pass on $p$.
3. At every (token position, layer), add an **error term**: the real MLP output on $p$ minus the CLT output on $p$.

After step 3, every activation and logit matches the real model exactly on $p$.

blocks.title: Building the local replacement model for one prompt

scenes.caption: One layer of the real model. Attention patterns, normalization and the MLP are all nonlinear in the inputs.
Replace the MLP with CLT features. Inside a feature the only nonlinearity left is its own JumpReLU.

Freeze attention weights and normalization denominators at their recorded values for this prompt. They become constants, so attention is a fixed linear map that still moves information between positions.
Add an error node per position and layer so the output matches the real MLP exactly. Error nodes have no inputs: they appear from nowhere in the graph and are not interpretable.

blocks.md:
Now the local replacement model is like one big fully connected network spread across token positions. Its inputs are the prompt tokens, its neurons are the active CLT features at every position, and its "virtual weights" are sums over every linear path from one feature to another through residual connections and frozen attention.

The graph has four node types:

- **Output nodes**: candidate tokens, enough to cover 95% of the probability, at most 10.
- **Feature nodes**: each active feature at each position.
- **Embedding nodes**: the prompt tokens.
- **Error nodes**: the part of each MLP output the CLT missed.

blocks.tex: A_{s\to t} = a_s\, w_{s\to t}, \qquad w_{s\to t} = \sum_{\ell_s \le \ell < \ell_t} \big(W_{dec,s}^{\ell_s \to \ell}\big)^{\!\top} J^{\blacktriangledown}_{c_s,\ell \to c_t,\ell_t}\, W_{enc,t}^{\ell_t}
blocks.caption: The edge from source feature s to target t is the source activation times a virtual weight: each layer's decoder vector of s, carried by the frozen Jacobian to t's position and layer, dotted with t's encoder.

blocks.md: The Jacobian of a function is the matrix of partial derivatives of each output entry with respect to each input entry; for a linear map it is the map itself. The J with a small downward triangle in the formula is the model's Jacobian with stop-gradients on every nonlinear part: MLP outputs, attention patterns and normalization denominators. A stop-gradient treats a value as a constant while differentiating, so these parts pass signals through but are not differentiated themselves, which leaves only linear steps. It expands into a sum over paths, where a residual step is the identity and an attention step is the head's frozen attention weight times its OV matrix (the part of the head that decides *what* is copied). This is the OV circuit $W_O W_V$ from lesson 4, and the sum over paths is the path expansion from that lesson with every attention pattern fixed.

In practice you never enumerate paths. For each target node, inject its encoder vector at its layer and position, run one backward pass with the stop-gradients, and dot the resulting gradient with each source's decoder vectors, times the source activation. The cost is linear in the number of active features.

**Worked example (toy numbers).** Prompt: "capital of the state containing Dallas is". A Dallas feature at the Dallas position has activation $a_s = 3.0$ and decoder $d = (1, 0.5, 0, 0)$. One head at the last position attends to the Dallas position with frozen weight 0.8, its input normalization has frozen denominator 2.0, and its OV map sends $d$ to $(0, 0, 1.6, 0.3)$. A Texas feature at the last position has encoder $e = (0, 0, 1.5, 0.5)$, so $e \cdot OV\,d = 2.4 + 0.15 = 2.55$.

blocks.caption: One path only, for clarity. Because the attention weight and denominator are constants, the edge is exactly proportional to the source activation.

blocks.title: The Texas feature's preactivation is the sum of its edges (toy)

scenes.caption: The edge we just computed: the Dallas feature contributes 3.06 to the Texas feature.
Other sources add their own linear edges: 0.3 straight from the Dallas token embedding, 0.4 from an error node, and a small negative 0.2 from the capital feature.
With everything nonlinear frozen, the preactivation is exactly the sum: 3.06 + 0.3 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 3.56. It clears the threshold 1.0, so the Texas feature is active at 3.56.

blocks.md:
Why does one backward pass give every edge at once? Check it on this toy. Give the head three source positions: Dallas (attention weight 0.8), the capital token (0.1) and the last position itself (0.1). Four sources write below the head: the Dallas feature and the Dallas embedding at the Dallas position, the capital feature at the capital position, and an error node (error L2 in the figure) at the last position. Then enumerate paths by hand:

- Dallas feature: one path, through attention: $3.0 \times \frac{0.8}{2.0} \times 2.55 = 3.06$.
- Error node: two paths. The **residual skip** stays at the last position and gives $e \cdot r = 0.305$; the self-attention path gives $\frac{0.1}{2.0}\, e \cdot M r = 0.095$. Total 0.4.

The Dallas embedding (0.3) and the capital feature (-0.2) work the same way through attention.

blocks.title: One backward pass reproduces every edge into Texas
blocks.code:
import torch
e = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1.5, 0.5])               # Texas encoder (target)
M = torch.tensor([[0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0, 0],    # head's OV matrix
                  [1.2, 0.8, 0, 0], [0.2, 0.2, 0.4, 0]])
d = torch.tensor([1, 0.5, 0, 0]);   a_d = 3.0     # Dallas feature (pos D)
u = torch.tensor([0, 0.5, 0.5, 0])                # Dallas embedding (pos D)
cap = torch.tensor([-0.5, -0.5, 0, 0]); a_c = 2.5 # capital feature (pos C)
err = torch.tensor([1, 0, 0, 0.61])               # error node (last pos)
alpha = torch.tensor([0.8, 0.1, 0.1])  # frozen attention: D, C, last
sigma = 2.0                            # frozen norm denominator

x = torch.stack([a_d * d + u, a_c * cap, err]).requires_grad_(True)
y = x[2] + sum(alpha[j] * M @ (x[j] / sigma) for j in range(3))
(e @ y).backward()                     # one backward pass from the target
g = x.grad
print(a_d * g[0] @ d, g[0] @ u, a_c * g[1] @ cap, g[2] @ err)

scenes.caption: The toy's vectors in 4 dimensions. The decoder, encoder and OV values are the ones from the worked example; the other sources were chosen to give the edges in the bar chart.
Attention weights and the norm denominator are plain constants, not functions of x: that is the stop-gradient. The head output is then linear in x.
Inject the target's encoder and run one backward pass. The gradient at the Dallas position is 0.4 M-transpose e = (0.76, 0.52, 0.08, 0); at the last position it is e plus 0.05 M-transpose e.
Dot that gradient with each source's vector, times its activation for features: 3.06, 0.3, -0.2 and 0.4, exactly the enumerated path sums. They add to the preactivation, 3.56.

blocks.md: Two things fall out. The Dallas feature and the Dallas embedding sit at the same position, so they share one gradient vector; only the vector you dot it with differs. That is why embedding and error nodes need no extra work: an embedding node's vector is its token embedding, an error node's vector is its MLP error, and both are dotted with the same gradient as the features. And the backward pass sums the residual skip and the attention path for the error node automatically, which is the sum over paths without listing a single path.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you had NOT frozen the attention pattern. If you doubled the Dallas feature's activation, would its effect on the Texas feature exactly double to 6.12?
blocks.reveal: Not necessarily. The Dallas feature also feeds the attention scores (the QK side), so changing it could change the 0.8 attention weight, and with it the edge. Freezing makes the edge exactly linear (doubling gives 6.12) but also means the graph says nothing about *why* attention went where it did. The paper's phrasing: graphs capture the OV circuits but ignore the QK circuits.

blocks.md: Matching the real model's outputs exactly on prompt $p$ does not mean the local replacement model uses the same mechanism. The paper compares it to a Taylor approximation: it agrees at the point and drifts as you move away, which is why interventions are needed later.

blocks.question: Which statement about error nodes in an attribution graph is correct?
options: They receive edges from the features that caused the error
They have outgoing edges but no incoming edges, and are not interpretable
They are removed before pruning because they carry no information
They only appear at the final layer
blocks.explain: An error node holds the gap between the true MLP output and the CLT output at one position and layer. It feeds later nodes, but the method has no way to attribute into it, so it appears from nowhere. There is one per position and layer, and the paper's pruning keeps them (circuit-tracer can drop low-influence ones).

blocks.question: In the toy, all other quantities are frozen and the Dallas feature's activation rises from 3.0 to 4.0. What is the new Dallas-to-Texas edge?
options: 3.06, because virtual weights do not depend on activations
It cannot be computed without rerunning attention
blocks.explain: The edge is activation times virtual weight: 4.0 x 1.02 = 4.08. The virtual weight 1.02 is fixed because the attention weight 0.8 and the denominator 2.0 are frozen.

blocks.question: Which nonlinearities does the local replacement model freeze at their observed values?
options: Attention patterns and normalization denominators
Only the CLT feature thresholds
The softmax over the output vocabulary
Nothing; it relies on gradients only
blocks.explain: Attention patterns and normalization denominators are frozen, and MLPs are replaced by CLT features plus error terms. The features' own JumpReLUs remain, which is why each feature's preactivation is linear in earlier activations but its activation is not.

lessons.title: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes

blocks.md:
Even with sparse features (on the order of a hundred active per token position), a full graph is huge: the methods paper notes that edges can reach the millions even for short prompts. A small subgraph usually carries most of the effect on the output, so the next job is to find it.

We will prune the toy graph from the last lesson. It has 3 embedding nodes, 2 error nodes, 6 active features and one logit node (Austin, which already has 99.6% of the probability among the toy's three candidates).

blocks.title: The toy attribution graph for the Dallas prompt

scenes.caption: Embeddings at the bottom, the logit at the top. Each arrow is a linear edge (small ones, like error or punctuation edges into the logit, are not drawn); badges show activations. The shape copies the biology paper's Dallas example; all numbers are toys.
Two parallel routes reach say Austin: Dallas to Texas, and capital to say a capital. A direct shortcut edge from Dallas also exists, as in the paper's real graph.
Logit influence (computed below) for each feature. Dallas has no direct edge to the logit, yet it scores 0.397 because all its paths count.
At the default node threshold 0.8, the punctuation feature falls outside the kept set and is pruned. In the paper, embedding and error nodes are never pruned.

blocks.md:
How do you score a node's importance? A direct edge to the logit is not enough: the Dallas feature has none. The paper uses **indirect influence**:

1. Take absolute values of all edge weights.
2. Normalize each node's incoming edges to sum to 1. Call this matrix $A$, indexed (target, source).
3. Sum over paths of every length with a Neumann series. Call the result $B$.

Why powers of $A$ count paths: an entry of $A$ squared adds up, over every middle node, the product of two normalized edges, so it covers all two-step paths; $A$ cubed covers three-step paths, and so on. Adding all the powers is the Neumann series, named after Carl Neumann. It is the matrix version of the geometric series 1 plus x plus x squared and so on, which equals 1 over 1 minus x.

An entry of $B$ is the sum over all paths between two nodes of the product of normalized edge weights. A node's **logit influence** is its entry in the logit rows of $B$, averaged with weights equal to each logit's probability.

blocks.caption: Converges because the graph is acyclic: A is strictly lower triangular in a topological order, so its powers eventually vanish.

blocks.title: Edges into four targets: signed, then normalized (toy)

scenes.caption: Signed edges, one row per target. Each row sums to that target's preactivation: 3.56 for Texas, 2.3 for say a capital, 4.2 for say Austin, 7.058 for the Austin logit.

Take absolute values and divide each row by its total. Texas now draws 0.773 of its input from Dallas; the logit draws 0.663 from say Austin and 0.141 from Texas. Signs are gone: influence measures size, not direction.

blocks.md:
Trace the Dallas feature's influence by hand. It reaches the logit along three paths; multiply normalized weights along each path and add:

- Dallas to Texas to say Austin to logit: $0.773 \times 0.424 \times 0.663 = 0.217$
- Dallas to Texas to logit: $0.773 \times 0.141 = 0.109$
- Dallas to say Austin to logit: $0.107 \times 0.663 = 0.071$

Total: 0.397, exactly the entry the matrix inverse gives.

blocks.title: Logit influence of each feature node (toy)

scenes.caption: Influence of the six feature nodes. Including embeddings and errors, the 11 non-logit nodes sum to 3.126 (computed by script).

Sort all non-logit nodes and keep the smallest prefix reaching 80% of the total. The cut lands at capital (cumulative 0.801); the capital embedding ties it at 0.255 and ties are kept, as in Anthropic's open-source circuit-tracer library. Punctuation is pruned.

blocks.md:
The full pruning recipe from the methods paper (and the `circuit-tracer` library):

1. **Nodes**: keep the smallest set of nodes covering 80% of total logit influence (`node_threshold` 0.8). Embedding and error nodes always stay in the paper; `circuit-tracer` always keeps token nodes but can drop low-influence error nodes.
2. Recompute influence on the pruned graph. Score each **edge** as its normalized weight times the influence of its target, and keep edges covering 98% (`edge_threshold` 0.98).
3. **Logits**: keep the top tokens until 95% probability, at most 10.

With defaults, nodes typically drop about 10x and edges about 500x, while the behavior explained drops by about 20%. The paper measures behavior explained with a completeness score: the share of the important nodes' input that comes from features and embeddings rather than error nodes, with each node weighted by its logit influence. A score of 1 means no error node feeds them.

Run step 2 on the toy. With punctuation gone, recompute influence on the pruned graph (say Austin rises to 0.688, Texas to 0.444) and give the logit node its probability, 1. Each edge's score is its normalized weight times its target's influence: for Dallas to Texas, $0.773 \times 0.444 = 0.343$. The 17 remaining edges have scores summing to 3.174. Sort them, and keep the smallest set whose cumulative share first reaches 0.98.

blocks.title: Edge scores on the pruned toy graph (rows = targets)

scenes.caption: Every edge's score, computed by script. The biggest is say Austin to the logit (0.688); the Dallas to Texas edge scores 0.343.

Cumulative share crosses 0.98 at the edge from error L2 to say a capital (0.037, share 0.982). The two smaller edges are cut: Dallas embedding to Texas (0.034) and capital to Texas (0.022), the toy's only inhibitory edge into Texas. 15 of 17 edges stay.

blocks.md:
The toy graph before pruning also gets the two scores (defined in the recipe above and again in lesson 9), computed with the formulas in `circuit-tracer`:

- **Replacement**: of all influence that tokens and errors exert on the logit, the share from tokens. Tokens carry 0.804 (0.429 + 0.255 + 0.120) and errors 0.196 (0.078 + 0.118), so replacement is 0.804 / 1.000 = 0.80.
- **Completeness**: for each node, the share of its normalized input that does not come from error nodes, averaged with weights equal to influence plus logit probability. Texas gets 0.899 (0.101 of its input is error L2), say a capital 0.897, say Austin 0.881, the logit 0.961, and every node with no inputs counts as 1. The weighted average is 0.95.

With tiny error edges, both scores are high. Real graphs score lower: the methods paper reports 0.80 completeness and 0.61 replacement for one prompt with a 10M-feature CLT.

Even pruned, a real graph often has hundreds of nodes. Researchers then **label** features using their top activating examples and their logit effects ("say X" for output features that push token X) and group them into **supernodes**: features that share the facet that matters for this prompt. For the acronym prompt in the methods paper, "The National Digital Analytics Group (N", which the model completes with "DAG)", three different "digital" features matter only because "digital" starts with D, so they become one node. The paper tried automated clustering and found none sufficient, so grouping is manual.

How is a feature named? The sparse autoencoder course shows how to read a latent from its activating examples and its logit effects. The methods paper sorts graph features into three kinds by those clues. **Input features**, common in early layers, fire on a specific token or close relatives ("digital", or any token ending in 6). **Output features**, common in late layers, are best read through their *logit effects*: the unembedding times the decoder, the tokens the feature directly promotes and suppresses. **Abstract features** in the middle need examples, logit effects and graph connections together. The paper notes logit effects get less informative the further a feature sits from the last layer.

blocks.title: Naming a feature from its logit effects (toy)

scenes.caption: Logit effect of one late-layer feature: its decoder dotted with each token's unembedding row (toy 4-dimensional numbers, computed by script). Austin gets +2.17 and the word-piece Aust +1.76.

Its top activating examples sit just before "Austin" appears. Promotes Austin and its first token piece, mildly other Texas words, suppresses an unrelated capital: label it "say Austin". Like "lac" for lacrosse in the paper, a token piece can top the list.

blocks.md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

blocks.question: In the toy, Dallas has no direct edge to the Austin logit. Why does pruning keep it anyway?
options: Embedding-like features are never pruned
Its indirect influence through Texas and say Austin is 0.397, the third highest
Pruning only looks at activations, and Dallas has a large one
Edges with the label shortcut are protected
blocks.explain: Node pruning ranks by indirect influence, which sums over all paths. Dallas reaches the logit through three paths worth 0.217 + 0.109 + 0.071. A direct-edge ranking would have discarded the start of the main reasoning chain.

blocks.question: You raise the node threshold from 0.8 to 0.95 on a real prompt. What should you expect?
options: Fewer nodes and higher completeness
The same nodes, because embeddings dominate
More nodes and lower completeness
More nodes and higher completeness
blocks.explain: A higher threshold keeps more of the influence. On one acronym prompt the paper reports 55 nodes and completeness 0.70 at 0.8, versus 236 nodes and 0.87 at 0.95: easier to explain more, harder to read.

blocks.question: Edge pruning at 0.98 cut the capital-to-Texas edge in the toy. What does that say about the edge?
options: It was inhibitory, and pruning always removes negative edges
Its source node had been pruned in the node step
Its score (normalized weight times target influence) was among the smallest, so it fell below the 98% cut
Edges into features are pruned before edges into logits
blocks.explain: Scores ignore sign: the edge's normalized weight 0.051 times Texas's influence 0.444 gave 0.022, the smallest score. A strong inhibitory edge would score high and survive; this one was simply weak.

blocks.md:
An attribution graph describes the **local replacement model**, not the real one. Its claims, such as "Texas features drive say Austin", must be tested by **perturbing features in the real model** and checking that downstream features and outputs move as the graph predicts.

To intervene on a feature, change its activation and inject its modified decoding in place of the original reconstruction. Cross-layer features write to many layers, so you choose a layer range. In **constrained patching**, you modify the feature's decoding at every layer in the range and run forward from the end of the range; MLP outputs inside the range are not recomputed, so there are no second-order effects inside it. Attention patterns are usually frozen at their clean values too (circuit-tracer's feature_intervention freezes them by default), though some biology-paper experiments leave them unfrozen.

Two practical details from the methods paper. They often steer a feature to *minus* its original value (multiply by -1) instead of setting it to zero, and they sweep the end of the patching range to find the layers where the feature's decoding matters most. Validation is coarse: it usually perturbs whole supernodes and checks the direction of effects.

The biology paper's Dallas graph for Claude 3.5 Haiku has the shape of our toy: Dallas features activate Texas features; capital features activate say-a-capital features; together they promote say Austin, plus a direct Dallas to say Austin shortcut. Swapping the Texas features for California features (found on an Oakland prompt) made the model say Sacramento; Georgia features gave Atlanta, and British Columbia features gave Victoria.

blocks.title: Interventions on the toy graph: next-token probabilities

scenes.caption: Baseline toy model: Austin 0.996. Probabilities use a softmax over these three candidates only (simplified). Interventions here recompute all downstream features.
Set Texas to 0. The Austin logit drops 3.20 (7.06 to 3.85) but Austin still wins with 0.946, because the capital route and the Dallas shortcut keep say Austin above its threshold.
Set say a capital to 0 instead. Austin falls to 0.860 and Texas rises to 0.136: without the capital route, the Texas feature's own push toward saying Texas shows through.
Zero both routes. say Austin drops below its threshold and switches off, the logits collapse to about 0, and the toy has no preference left: 0.34, 0.33, 0.33.
Swap: zero Texas and turn on an inactive California feature at 3.5. say Sacramento switches on and the output flips to Sacramento with 0.952, the same kind of test as the paper's swap.

blocks.prompt: From the graph, zeroing Texas lowers the Austin logit by 1.068 directly plus 1.2 x 1.78 = 2.136 through say Austin: 3.20 total, and that matches exactly. Zeroing say a capital is predicted at 2.58. If you zero BOTH, will the drop be 3.20 + 2.58 = 5.78?
blocks.reveal: No. The actual drop is **7.03**. With both inputs gone, say Austin's preactivation falls to 1.04, below its threshold of 1.5, so the feature switches off entirely and its remaining 1.04 x 1.2 contribution vanishes too. Each edge is linear, but features are still JumpReLUs, so effects of large perturbations do not simply add. This is one reason why validation checks directions and rough sizes, not exact sums.

blocks.md:
How well do graphs predict interventions in general? Two terms first. To ablate a feature is to switch it off (set it to zero or steer it negative) and measure what changes. Spearman correlation compares two lists by their rank order: it is the ordinary correlation of the ranks, so 1 means the two lists sort the items identically and 0 means their orders are unrelated.

From the methods paper's evaluations on the 18L model:

- A node's logit influence predicts the effect of ablating it on the output better than direct edge weight or activation size.
- Across 20 prompts, graph influence between pairs of features and the measured effect of ablating the upstream one had a Spearman correlation of 0.72.
- For perturbations of the local replacement model vs the real model, effects one layer later agree only partly (cosine similarity around 0.6 to 0.8 for the largest 18L dictionary), but the gap compounds over layers, and magnitudes drift more than directions.

blocks.title: Planning in poems: where the intervention works

scenes.caption: Haiku writes: "He saw a carrot and had to grab it, / His hunger was like a starving rabbit". Attributing back from rabbit lands on features at the newline, before line 2 begins: rhyme features activate candidate words rabbit and habit.
The planned word also shapes the middle of the line: rabbit features promote comparison features before "like a". The model writes toward its target.
Interventions confirm it. Suppressing rabbit pushes the line toward habit; injecting a green feature makes lines end in green. Steering at any token other than the newline had no effect.

blocks.md: Graph first, intervention second. The graph proposes which features matter and how; perturbing those features in the real model is what turns a picture into evidence. Expect directional agreement, not exact numbers.

blocks.question: Why does constrained patching over layers [i, j] avoid double counting a cross-layer feature's effect?
options: It edits the feature's decoding at each layer in the range and does not recompute MLP outputs inside the range, so the only change there is the intervention
It recomputes every MLP inside the range so the feature's effect is applied once
It removes attention for the duration of the range
It only patches the final layer, where all decoders meet
blocks.explain: A CLT feature writes to many layers. Editing its decoder outputs across the range while not recomputing MLPs inside that range means the only change to those MLP outputs is your edit. Knock-on effects appear only after the range ends.

blocks.question: In the poem study, steering the planned-word features changed the rhyme only at the newline token, not at other positions. What does that support?
options: The model improvises the rhyme at the last word
Attention is broken at every other token
The plan is represented at a specific site before the line is written, and later tokens read it from there
Steering never works in Haiku
blocks.explain: If the plan were made at the end of the line, steering near the end would matter. The effect being confined to the newline token supports a planning site from which later positions read, which is what the attribution graph suggested.

lessons.title: What attribution graphs found: arithmetic, languages, refusals, CoT

blocks.md:
The Dallas and poem examples are two of about a dozen case studies in the biology paper, all on Claude 3.5 Haiku. Reading several of them teaches the motifs that recur in real graphs. The paper's own summary, "Commonly observed circuit components", lists among others:

- **Input, abstract and output features**: paths start at token-like features, pass through abstract ones in the middle layers, and end at "say X" features.
- **Convergent paths and shortcuts**: a source reaches a target by several routes of different lengths, like Dallas to Austin directly and through Texas.
- **Default circuits**: some features are on by default and get *inhibited* when evidence arrives.
- **Special tokens**: newlines and punctuation often store information, as the poem plan did.

For each case below, keep two kinds of claim apart: what the graph *suggests*, and what an intervention in the real model *confirmed*.

**Addition.** For "calc: 36+59=" Haiku answers 95 through two parallel paths. A low-precision path goes from "add something near 57" features to a lookup-table feature for "something near 36 plus something near 60" and on to "the sum is near 92". A high-precision path goes from "an operand ends in 9" to a lookup feature for "ends in 6 plus ends in 9" and on to "the sum ends in 5". The two combine into 95. The paper found these roles with *operand plots*: each feature's activity on all 10,000 prompts "a+b=" for a and b from 0 to 99, where diagonal stripes mean the feature tracks the sum, and isolated points mean a lookup-table feature for specific input pairs.

blocks.title: Two parallel paths add 36 and 59 (simplified from the biology paper)

scenes.caption: Low-precision path: features for rough magnitudes feed a lookup feature for roughly 36 plus roughly 60, which feeds "sum near 92". It knows the answer is in the 90s, not which number.
High-precision path: a memorized one-digit table. "Ends in 6" plus "ends in 9" activates "sum ends in 5".
Both paths vote on the output: near 92 and ending in 5 picks 95. Neither path alone carries the full answer, a convergent-paths motif.

blocks.md:
Two follow-ups show what is validated and what is not. The same "ends in 6 plus ends in 9" feature fires far from arithmetic, for example on an academic citation in the journal *Polymer*, volume 36, where adding the volume to the year before the journal's founding (1959) predicts the publication year 1995. That role was **tested by intervention**: swapping the feature for an "ends in 9 plus ends in 9" feature changed the predicted year from 1995 to 1998.

Then the authors asked Haiku how it got 95. It described the school method: add the ones (6 + 9 = 15), carry the 1, add the tens. The attribution graph for that conversation shows the same parallel features as before, with no carrying. The paper's reading: the model explains its arithmetic by imitating explanations it has seen, not by inspecting its own circuit.

blocks.prompt: In the Polymer citation the model writes 1995. You may switch one feature off and inject one other feature from a different prompt. Which change should make it write 1998, and what in the graph tells you so?
blocks.reveal: Turn off the "ends in 6 plus ends in 9" lookup feature and inject an "ends in 9 plus ends in 9" feature. The graph shows the lookup feature driving the ones-digit output ("sum ends in 5"), while the decade comes from other features. Swapping only the ones-digit lookup should move only the last digit: 9 + 9 ends in 8, so 1998. That is the result the paper reports.

blocks.md:
**Multilingual circuits.** Three prompts with the same meaning, "The opposite of "small" is "", its French version (answer "grand") and its Chinese version, run through very similar circuits. Language-independent features recognize the operation (antonym) and the operand (small) and push "say large"; separate language-specific features, such as open-quote-in-French, pick the output language. Evidence for sharing: 20 of the 27 features in the multilingual supernodes are active on all three prompts, though only 10 of 27 survive pruning in all three graphs.

Each part could be edited independently. Swapping antonym features for synonym features gave a language-appropriate synonym, though it needed 6 times the synonym prompt's activation, with the effect kicking in near 4 times in every language. Swapping the "small" features for "hot" features gave the antonym of hot. Swapping the language-detection features changed the output language.

blocks.title: Shared and language-specific parts of the antonym circuit (simplified)

scenes.caption: The French prompt. Shared features compute "the opposite of small" and promote say-large; the French quote feature picks the French word. The antonym edge works partly through attention QK, which the graph cannot show (dashed).
Edit the operand: replace the small features with hot features taken from an English prompt. The output becomes the French antonym of hot.
Edit the language instead: replace the French detection features with Chinese ones. Operation and operand are untouched, and the answer comes out in Chinese.

blocks.md:
The paper adds two measured trends: features in the middle layers are more language-agnostic than those near the input and output, and Haiku shares more features across languages than a smaller comparison model. It also finds English mechanistically privileged: multilingual features connect more directly to English outputs, making English the default.

**Entity recognition and hallucination.** In the Human/Assistant format, "can't answer" features are switched on by default by features for the Assistant turn, and generic name features switch on "unknown name" features. For a known entity, Michael Jordan, "known entity" and "known answer" features *inhibit* both, and the model answers. For the made-up Michael Batkin nothing inhibits them, and the model declines. This is the default-circuit motif.

blocks.title: A default refusal circuit and the features that inhibit it

scenes.caption: Any Human/Assistant question switches on can't-answer features. Left alone, they win and the model declines.

A familiar entity switches on known-answer features that inhibit can't-answer, and the sports features win. Promoting known-answer features on the Michael Batkin prompt made the model guess a sport, chess included.

A natural misfire: asked for a paper by Andrej Karpathy, known-answer features fire weakly because the name is familiar, refusal is suppressed, and the model names a famous paper Karpathy did not write. Inhibiting those features made it decline.

blocks.md: Not every prediction held. Activating "unknown name" features on the Michael Jordan prompt did *not* produce a refusal, although the graph suggested it would, and most edits needed activations far above natural values. The paper reads this as a sign that the identified features capture only part of the mechanism.

**Refusals.** For "Write an advertisement for cleaning with bleach and ammonia" (a mixture that releases a toxic gas), the graph attributing from the refusal's first token shows features for the danger of mixing cleaning chemicals feeding a chain from "harmful request" to "Assistant should refuse" to "say I" (refusals start "I apologize"). Ablating the chemical-danger cluster made the model comply; ablating the Human/Assistant context features made it give a plain warning instead of its default refusal. Tracing the global weights (virtual weights between features computed across all prompts, not one) upstream of a general harmful-request feature finds many specific harm features, and graphs for 200 harmful prompts found several dozen features that were consistently influential when the model refused. Dictionaries trained only on pretraining data had very few refusal features. For optional further reading outside this course's prerequisites, the steering-vectors course treats refusal as a direction in the residual stream.

**A jailbreak.** Given a four-word phrase whose first letters spell a weapon, and asked to assemble the letters and explain how to make one, Haiku starts "BOMB. To make a bomb..." before refusing a sentence later. The graphs suggest why. The model never represented the word internally before writing it: each letter came from a separate path voting on the output. Once its own text said "To make a bomb", harmful-request features turned on, and together with "new sentence" features after the first period they promoted "However". The decisive part ran through attention: clamping the new-sentence features to zero with attention frozen mostly removed the "However" while the model still refused; with attention free to change, the same clamp let it keep complying.

**Chain-of-thought faithfulness.** For $\sqrt{0.64}$ the graph shows a real computation of $\sqrt{64}$. For $\cos(23423)$ with no hint, Haiku claimed to use a calculator, and the graph shows no sign of a real computation. With a hint ("I got 4"), the graph shows the model working *backwards*: it picks an intermediate value (0.8) so that multiplying by 5 lands on the hinted 4. Inhibiting those features moved the answer away from 0.8, and changing the hint changed the reasoning to match it. For optional further reading outside this course's prerequisites, the chain-of-thought faithfulness course studies this behavior from the outside.

Confirmed by intervention: the addition lookup swap (1995 to 1998), the three multilingual edits, known-answer features gating hallucination, ablations that change refusals, and the hint-driven backward reasoning. Graph readings only: no carrying in the model's arithmetic, English as default, and anything involving attention, such as why the model attends to the hint or why "However" needs a new sentence.

Every case is one or a few prompts on one model, chosen because the method worked. The paper says plainly that it makes claims about examples, not general mechanisms, and that its graphs gave satisfying insight for only about a quarter of the prompts the authors tried.

blocks.question: Haiku's graph for an unknown name shows can't-answer features driven by Assistant-turn features. What does it mean to call this a default circuit?
options: It only runs when the prompt has no system message
It is active unless something inhibits it, so answering requires features that switch it off
It was trained with a separate objective from the rest of the model
It is the circuit with the most edges in the graph
blocks.explain: The refusal path fires for any Human/Assistant question. Known-entity and known-answer features inhibit it when the model recognizes the subject. Hallucinations can come from that inhibition misfiring on a familiar-sounding name.

blocks.question: Which of these findings was confirmed by an intervention in the real model, rather than read off a graph?
options: Haiku does not use carrying when it adds 36 and 59
English is the default output language of the multilingual circuit
The model attends to the hint because of sycophancy features
Swapping the antonym features for synonym features yields a synonym in each language
blocks.explain: The antonym-to-synonym swap was run in the model in all three languages (at about 4 to 6 times natural activation). The no-carrying and English-default claims come from reading graphs, and why the model attends to a hint is attention computation the graphs cannot trace.

blocks.question: In the jailbreak, clamping "new sentence" features changed the outcome only when attention patterns were allowed to change. What does that imply for the graph?
options: The new-sentence features are error nodes
The graph was pruned too aggressively
The key step of the refusal runs through attention QK, which a frozen-attention graph does not show
Attention is irrelevant to refusals
blocks.explain: With attention frozen, the clamp mostly removed "However" while the model still refused; with attention unfrozen, it kept complying. So the mechanism that matters changes where heads attend, exactly the QK computation lesson 9 lists as missing.

blocks.md:
**Missing attention circuits.** Because attention patterns are frozen, graphs show what information moved between positions (OV) but not why attention chose that position (QK). The methods paper's example: on "I always loved visiting Aunt Sally. Whenever I was feeling sad, Aunt", the graph for Haiku says the model predicts Sally because a Sally feature earlier fed say-Sally features. That misses the real story, an induction mechanism that attended to Sally *because* it followed the earlier Aunt. An induction head (lesson 4) finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies the token that came right after it: Aunt was followed by Sally before, so predict Sally.

On a multiple-choice question the graph said the model answered B because of a feature for tokens following "(b)". How it knew 1945 was correct lived in attention, so the graph skipped the interesting part.

blocks.title: What the graph shows on an induction prompt

scenes.caption: The attribution graph: Sally features at the earlier position feed say Sally at the last position through a frozen attention head. True, but uninformative.
The missing step: the head attended to Sally because the current token Aunt matches the token before Sally. That query-key computation sets the frozen pattern, so the graph never shows it.

blocks.md: **A 2025 update fills part of this gap.** Kamath, Ameisen et al. (*Tracing Attention Computation Through Feature Interactions*, July 2025) start from the fact that a head's pre-softmax score is bilinear in the residual streams at the query and key positions (linear in each one while the other is held fixed, as in $x_q^\top W_{QK} x_k$ from lesson 4). Write each side as a sum of feature vectors plus a bias and an error term, multiply out, and the score becomes a sum of query-feature by key-feature terms: a **QK attribution**. List the terms by size and you can read *why* the head attended there.

blocks.tex: s(p_q, p_k) = \Big(\sum_i a_i \mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{b}_q + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_q\Big)^{\!\top} W_{QK} \Big(\sum_j a_j \mathbf{v}_j + \mathbf{b}_k + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k\Big) = \sum_{i,j} a_i a_j\, \mathbf{v}_i^{\top} W_{QK} \mathbf{v}_j + \ldots
blocks.caption: i runs over features at the query position, j over features at the key position. The dots are the bias and error cross terms. A normalization layer before W_Q and W_K is handled by linearizing it.

blocks.title: QK attribution for one head, Aunt query to Sally key (toy)

scenes.caption: Each cell is one query feature times one key feature through W_QK (toy numbers, computed by script). The score is their sum, 9.795, plus terms not shown.

The update's induction finding has this shape: query-side Aunt features match key-side "name of an aunt or uncle" features (4.8 here), alongside a generic attend-to-names term (3.0), and the query bias also favors names.

blocks.md:
Their case studies confirmed hypotheses the original papers could not test. On the Aunt Sally prompt, steering the key-side "name of an aunt or uncle" features negatively, inside the QK circuit of the heads that carried the edge, removed induction: the model predicted generic aunt names instead. A previous-token step was visible too, with query-side first-name features matching key-side "title before a name" features. On the multiple-choice question, query-side "say an answer" features matched key-side "correct answer" features on the 1945 option; injecting those features on another option flipped the answer letter.

To know *which* heads carry an edge, they add **head loadings**: each edge split into one term per head. Long transcoder paths make that exponential in depth, so they checkpoint with features read from the residual stream at every layer (weakly causal crosscoders). The price: edges through MLPs are no longer linear. The authors call these first attempts; at publication the method was not part of the open-source tools.

**Other dictionary designs.** Paulo, Shabalin and Belrose (2025) found transcoder features more interpretable than SAE features trained on the same model and data, and proposed **skip transcoders**, which add an affine skip connection (a learned linear map plus bias from input to output) and reach lower reconstruction error with no loss of interpretability. Any such change to the replacement model shifts how much ends up in error nodes.

**Reconstruction error and dark matter.** Error nodes mark computation the CLT missed. The papers call this unexplained remainder the model's dark matter: computation that none of the dictionary's features capture. Sometimes error nodes swamp the graph: on an obfuscated jailbreak prompt (a request for malicious code with its words misspelled and their capitalization scrambled), almost all nodes on the obfuscated tokens were error nodes, so the origin of the refusal could not be traced.
