Two scores track this. **Completeness**, from lesson 6, gives partial credit: each important node counts for the part of its input that avoids error nodes. **Replacement** is the share of full embedding-to-logit paths that avoid error nodes entirely (only complete explanations count).

blocks.title: Graph scores on one example prompt, 10M dictionaries (methods paper)

scenes.caption: On one representative prompt in the methods paper (not a dataset average), completeness is similar: 0.80 with a 10M-feature CLT and 0.78 with 10M per-layer transcoders (PLTs).
Replacement score separates them: 0.61 vs 0.37. Shorter CLT paths cross fewer error nodes, so more end-to-end paths are fully explained.

blocks.md: **Inactive features and inhibition.** Graphs show only active features, but sometimes what matters is a feature that was *suppressed*. The entity circuit from lesson 8 is the clearest case: whether Haiku answers depends on "can't answer" features being switched *off* by known-entity features. Explaining a hallucination means explaining why "can't answer" was *off*, which a graph of active features does not show. The authors found the relevant features with contrastive pairs of prompts.

**Also:** graphs can be too complex to read; features can sit at the wrong level of abstraction (splitting, absorption). Absorption is when a specific feature takes over part of a general one: a "starts with S" feature may fail to fire on "short" because a "short" feature already carries that information. Global weights, the virtual weights between features across all prompts rather than one, are full of interference: features that never fire together on real text can still have large virtual weights between them, connections that never affect what the network does (a July 2025 Anthropic note builds toy models of these interference weights); and the CLT may not use the same mechanism as the MLPs it replaces.

An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

**Doing it yourself.** In May 2025 Anthropic open-sourced the method as [circuit-tracer](https://github.com/decoderesearch/circuit-tracer), developed by Anthropic Fellows Michael Hanna and Mateusz Piotrowski, and [Neuronpedia](https://www.neuronpedia.org/gemma-2-2b/graph) (run by Decode Research) hosts a frontend where you can generate a graph, group supernodes and steer features without installing anything. The library computes the graph, prunes it, serves the same viewer as the papers, and runs interventions. Its README lists transcoders for open models such as Gemma 2 2B and Llama 3.2 1B, plus newer sets for Qwen 3 and Gemma 3; Gemma 2 2B runs within a free Colab GPU's 15GB. The next lesson is a full lab with it.

blocks.code:
import torch
from circuit_tracer import ReplacementModel, attribute
from circuit_tracer.utils import create_graph_files

# Gemma 2 2B with the GemmaScope per-layer transcoders ("gemma" preset)
model = ReplacementModel.from_pretrained(
    "google/gemma-2-2b", "gemma", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

prompt = "Fact: the capital of the state containing Dallas is"
graph = attribute(prompt=prompt, model=model,
                  max_n_logits=10,          # at most 10 logit nodes
                  desired_logit_prob=0.95,  # ...or fewer if 95% is covered
                  batch_size=256, max_feature_nodes=8192)
graph.to_pt("dallas.pt")

# prune (node 0.8, edge 0.98) and write files for the graph viewer
create_graph_files(graph_or_path="dallas.pt", slug="dallas-austin",
                   output_path="./graph_files",
                   node_threshold=0.8, edge_threshold=0.98)
blocks.caption: Adapted from the circuit-tracer demo notebooks: attribute one prompt, then prune and write files for the graph viewer. The lab in the next lesson adds labeling and interventions.

blocks.title: How circuit-tracer orders nodes in graph.adjacency_matrix

scenes.caption: A tiny example: 3 active features, 2 layers, 3 positions, 2 logit targets. Rows of the matrix are targets and columns are sources, in this order.
First come the active features kept in the graph (graph.selected_features, which index rows of graph.active_features given as (layer, position, feature index)).
Then one error node per layer per position: n_layers x n_pos = 2 x 3 = 6 entries.
Then one embedding node per token position, and last the logit nodes. Entry [target, source] is the direct effect of the source on the target with attention, norms and other features held fixed.

blocks.question: A graph for a multiple-choice question says the model answered B because of a "tokens following (b)" feature. What is the most likely reason the graph misses how the model knew B was right?
options: The CLT was too small to have a 1945 feature
The deciding computation is in the attention pattern (QK), which the method freezes and does not attribute
Pruning at 0.8 always removes the answer features
Logit nodes only cover the top token
blocks.explain: Freezing attention makes edges linear but means the graph explains what moved, not why attention moved it. The paper found that freezing attention locked the answer, so the crux was in the QK computation.

blocks.question: Graph A has completeness 0.80 and replacement 0.61; graph B has 0.78 and 0.37. What does B's lower replacement score mean?
options: Fewer of B's full paths from embeddings to the logit avoid error nodes
B's features are less interpretable
B used a higher pruning threshold
B's logits are wrong
blocks.explain: Both have most node inputs explained (completeness), but replacement only credits complete embedding-to-logit paths that never pass through an error node. Longer per-layer paths have more chances to hit one.

blocks.question: To explain why a model hallucinated about an unknown name, which approach does the biology paper suggest is needed beyond a single attribution graph?
options: Raise the pruning threshold until the cause appears
Remove all error nodes
Compare contrastive prompts (known vs unknown entity) to find features that should have been active but were suppressed
Use only direct edges to the logit
blocks.explain: Graphs list active features. A hallucination can come from a "can't answer" feature being wrongly inhibited, so you need a counterfactual (Michael Jordan vs Michael Batkin) to find the inactive feature and its inhibitors.

lessons.title: Lab: trace, label and intervene on a real graph with circuit-tracer

blocks.md:
This lab runs the whole loop on an open model: attribute, read the scores, rank and label features, group a supernode, intervene, and report. It uses Gemma 2 2B with the GemmaScope per-layer transcoders (GemmaScope is Google DeepMind's open release of SAEs and transcoders trained on Gemma 2) through the `circuit-tracer` library. Its README says Gemma 2 2B works within a free Colab GPU's 15GB. The model is gated on Hugging Face, so accept its license and log in first. Install the library as its README says (clone the repository, then `pip install .`). Its default backend imports TransformerLens's `HookedTransformer`, which TransformerLens 4 removed, so also pin `transformer-lens<4` or pass `backend="nnsight"`.

The code was **not run here** (no NVIDIA GPU on this machine). The numbers quoted come from the library's published tutorial notebook, which runs the same Dallas interventions on the same model and transcoders.

blocks.code:
import torch
from circuit_tracer import ReplacementModel, attribute
from circuit_tracer.graph import compute_graph_scores, compute_node_influence

# Gemma 2 2B with the GemmaScope per-layer transcoders ("gemma" preset)
model = ReplacementModel.from_pretrained("google/gemma-2-2b", "gemma",
                                         dtype=torch.bfloat16)
prompt = "Fact: the capital of the state containing Dallas is"
graph = attribute(prompt=prompt, model=model, max_n_logits=10,
                  desired_logit_prob=0.95, batch_size=256)
graph.to_pt("dallas.pt")
replacement, completeness = compute_graph_scores(graph)
print(f"replacement {replacement:.2f}  completeness {completeness:.2f}")
blocks.caption: Step 1: attribute one prompt and score the graph. compute_graph_scores returns the replacement and completeness scores from lesson 6. Not run here.

blocks.md: Read the two scores before anything else. Completeness says how much of the important nodes' input comes from features and tokens rather than error nodes; replacement credits only full token-to-logit paths that avoid errors. The toy graph in lesson 6 scored 0.95 and 0.80; the methods paper's example scored 0.80 and 0.61 with a 10M-feature CLT and 0.78 and 0.37 with per-layer transcoders. GemmaScope transcoders are per-layer, so expect replacement to suffer from long paths. The README also lists cross-layer transcoders for Gemma 2 2B (426K and 2.5M features) if you want to compare. A graph whose important nodes are mostly fed by errors cannot support a confident story.

blocks.title: Step 2: rank feature nodes by logit influence (not run here)
blocks.code:
n_feat = len(graph.selected_features)
A = graph.adjacency_matrix                  # rows = targets, cols = sources
w = torch.zeros(A.shape[0], device=A.device)
w[-len(graph.logit_targets):] = graph.logit_probabilities
infl = compute_node_influence(A, w)         # logit influence of every node
for i in infl[:n_feat].topk(10).indices.tolist():
    j = graph.selected_features[i]          # index into active_features
    layer, pos, feat = graph.active_features[j].tolist()
    act = graph.activation_values[j].item()
    print(f"{layer}_{feat}_{pos}  act {act:6.1f}  influence {infl[i]:.3f}")

scenes.caption: Node order in the adjacency matrix: selected features first, then error nodes, token nodes and logit nodes (the layout from lesson 9). n_feat counts the feature block.
Logit weights: zero everywhere except the logit nodes, which get their probabilities. Influence is then the Neumann-series sum from lesson 6, computed by repeated multiplication.
Map each top node back to (layer, position, feature index) and its activation. selected_features indexes into active_features and activation_values, which list every active feature.
Printed ids use Neuronpedia's layer_feature_position format, so you can paste them into its graph viewer and read each feature's examples and logit effects.
scenes.output: (not run here: prints ten lines of the form layer_feature_pos, activation, influence)

blocks.md:
**Label and group.** Open the graph on Neuronpedia (the annotated Dallas graph is linked at the top of the tutorial notebook) or serve it locally with `create_graph_files`. For each top node, read its activating examples and logit effects, as the sparse autoencoder course shows for SAE latents, and its strongest edges. Then group features that play the same role on this prompt into a supernode, requiring that they push the same downstream nodes with the same sign.

The published annotation of this graph has a Texas supernode of six features, all at position 9 (the Dallas token, counting the start token as 0): layer 20 feature 15589, 19/7477, 16/25, 4/13154, 14/2268 and 7/6861. It also has capital, state and say-a-capital supernodes, and a single say-Austin feature (layer 23, feature 12237, position 10).

blocks.code:
# Texas supernode from the annotated Neuronpedia graph: (layer, pos, feature)
texas = [(20, 9, 15589), (19, 9, 7477), (16, 9, 25),
         (4, 9, 13154), (14, 9, 2268), (7, 9, 6861)]
logits, acts = model.get_activations(prompt)
interventions = [(l, p, f, -2 * acts[l, p, f]) for (l, p, f) in texas]
new_logits, new_acts = model.feature_intervention(prompt, interventions)

def top5(lg):
    v, i = lg[0, -1].softmax(-1).topk(5)
    return [(model.tokenizer.decode(t), round(p, 2))
            for p, t in zip(v.tolist(), i.tolist())]
print(top5(logits)); print(top5(new_logits))

# swap: California features from the Oakland prompt, at 2x their activation
oakland = "Fact: the capital of the state containing Oakland is"
_, cal_acts = model.get_activations(oakland)
california = [(22, 10, 4367), (21, 10, 2464), (6, 9, 13909),
              (8, 9, 14641), (14, 9, 12562)]
swap = interventions + [(l, p, f, 2 * cal_acts[l, p, f]) for (l, p, f) in california]
print(top5(model.feature_intervention(prompt, swap)[0]))
blocks.caption: Step 3: intervene. Each tuple is (layer, position, feature index, new value); here each Texas feature is set to minus twice its own activation, as in the tutorial. feature_intervention freezes attention by default. Not run here.

blocks.title: Top-5 next tokens on Gemma 2 2B (published tutorial run)

scenes.caption: Baseline: Austin 0.42, then "not" 0.06, "the" 0.06, Texas 0.05, Fort 0.04. Gemma 2 2B is far less confident than Haiku.
Texas supernode at -2x: Austin drops out of the top 5. Now "the" 0.08, Albany 0.07, Harrisburg 0.06, Hartford 0.05, "not" 0.05. Without Texas, the model still says some state capital.
Say-a-capital supernode at -2x instead: Texas 0.45, then "the" 0.08, "called" 0.05, "not" 0.05, "known" 0.03. The state survives; the capital step is gone, as in the biology paper.
Swap: Texas at -2x plus the California supernode at 2x. Sacramento 0.37, "the" 0.06, "not" 0.04, a whitespace token 0.02, Olympia 0.02.

blocks.title: Downstream supernodes, as % of their normal activation (same run)

scenes.caption: Clamp say-a-capital to -200% (-2x). Say Austin falls to 0%: the graph's edge from say-a-capital to say Austin is real.
Clamp Texas to -2x. Say a capital is untouched (102%) but say Austin drops to 28%, matching the graph: Texas feeds say Austin, not say a capital.
Clamp capital to -2x: say a capital falls to 23% and say Austin to 57%, an upstream effect diluted by other inputs. State and Texas stay near normal (91%, 98%).
Clamp state to -2x: everything stays near 100% and Austin is still top at 0.36. A supernode the graph includes can still have little causal effect, so test each one.

blocks.md:
Not every swap works. The tutorial's British Columbia supernode (from "... the territory containing Vancouver is"), injected at 2x after removing Texas, left the outputs looking like plain Texas removal (Albany, Harrisburg, Hartford) and its say-Victoria feature stayed at 0%. A failed swap is a result: the features may not carry the facet you assumed, the strength may be too low, or the circuit may differ for that entity.

**Reporting checklist.** When you write up a circuit, state:

1. The exact prompt, model, and dictionary (name, size, per-layer or cross-layer).
2. Completeness and replacement scores, and the pruning thresholds you used.
3. Each supernode's member features, with the evidence for its label.
4. Which edges you validated, with the intervention (layers, positions, values, attention frozen or not) and the measured effect, including failures.
5. Which important paths pass through error nodes, and anything that depends on attention.
Graph, then labels, then interventions, then a report that names its own gaps. The graph proposes; only the measured change in the real model, including the swaps that fail, counts as evidence.

blocks.question: After clamping a supernode to -2x, the model's top output does not change and downstream supernodes stay near 100%. What is the best conclusion?
options: The intervention code is broken, since the graph showed the node
This supernode has little causal effect on this output, even though the pruned graph kept it
Attention must be unfrozen for any intervention to work
The node should be relabeled as an error node
blocks.explain: The state supernode in the tutorial behaves this way. Influence ranks nodes inside the replacement model; the intervention measures the real model. A kept node with no measurable effect is a finding to report, not something to hide.

blocks.question: Your graph has completeness 0.55 and most input to the say-answer features comes from error nodes. What should you do before telling a story about the circuit?
options: Raise the node threshold until the error nodes disappear
Report the story but omit the scores
Delete error nodes from the adjacency matrix and recompute influence
Treat the explanation as incomplete: try a larger or cross-layer dictionary, or another prompt, and say which paths go through errors
blocks.explain: Error nodes are computation the dictionary missed. Pruning keeps them in the paper's method, and deleting them hides the gap. A better dictionary (more features or a CLT) or a less unusual prompt can raise completeness; either way, the report should say where the explanation stops.
